source_semantics.question: Let a degree-d polynomial be given by Bernstein coefficients c(0),...,c(d), all lying in a common interval [lo, hi]. Suppose we restrict the polynomial to a subinterval [u, v] with 0 <= u < v <= 1 by two successive de Casteljau subdivisions, producing new Bernstein coefficients c'(0),...,c'(d) for the restricted piece. Prove that every restricted coefficient c'(i) still lies in [lo, hi]. Identify the two structural facts about the Bernstein basis that make this true.
source_semantics.reference_answer: Two facts drive the proof. Fact A (partition of unity): the Bernstein basis functions of a fixed degree sum to 1 at every t, i.e. sum_{r=0}^{d} B_{d,r}(t) = 1. Fact B (nonnegativity on [0,1]): each B_{d,r}(t) >= 0 for t in [0,1]. Together they say that any Bernstein sum sum_r c(r) B_{d,r}(t) with t in [0,1] is a convex combination of the c(r), hence lies between min and max of the coefficients; in particular if all c(r) in [lo,hi] the value lies in [lo,hi]. Step 1 (one subdivision preserves bounds): each new coefficient produced by a single de Casteljau subdivision at a parameter in [0,1] is itself a Bernstein sum of a sub-row of the original coefficients evaluated at that parameter. By Facts A and B it is a convex combination of coefficients from [lo,hi], hence in [lo,hi]. This applies to the right-edge (upper) subdivision at u in [0,1]: all its outputs stay in [lo,hi]. Step 2 (second subdivision): the left-edge (lower) subdivision is applied at the parameter (v-u)/(1-u). Because 0 <= u < v <= 1 we have 0 <= (v-u)/(1-u) <= 1 (the numerator is nonnegative and at most the positive denominator 1-u). So the second subdivision is again evaluated at a parameter in [0,1], and by the same convex-combination argument its outputs — the restricted coefficients c'(i) — remain in [lo,hi]. Step 3 (conclusion): composing the two bound-preserving subdivisions keeps every c'(i) in [lo,hi]. This is the exact numerical-stability property of de Casteljau subdivision: restricting to a subinterval never amplifies coefficients beyond the original range, in contrast to monomial-basis restriction which can.

source_semantics.question: A reversible source-loader on three little-endian bits is defined by the rule that maps each slot value s in {0,...,7} to (s XOR 3) mod 8, i.e. it flips the two low-order bits of s. Prove that this loader is its own inverse (an involution) as a permutation of {0,...,7}, and give the explicit image list obtained by applying it to 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 in order. Explain why the involution property is exactly what lets the two bit-flip gates that realize it also undo it when applied a second time.
source_semantics.reference_answer: The loader is L(s) = (s XOR 3) mod 8. Since every s in {0,...,7} is below 8, the outer mod 8 is inert and L(s) = s XOR 3. Bitwise XOR with the fixed mask 3 (binary 011) toggles bit 0 and bit 1 and leaves bit 2 untouched. XOR with a fixed mask is self-inverse because XOR is associative and commutative with x XOR x = 0: L(L(s)) = (s XOR 3) XOR 3 = s XOR (3 XOR 3) = s XOR 0 = s, so L is an involution and in particular a bijection of the 8-element set. Applying L to 0..7 in order gives [3, 2, 1, 0, 7, 6, 5, 4]: 0->3, 1->2, 2->1, 3->0, 4->7, 5->6, 6->5, 7->4. Operationally the loader is implemented by two X (bit-flip) gates on wires 0 and 1; because each X is self-inverse and the two flips commute, running the same two gates again applies 3 XOR 3 = 0, returning every slot to its original value, which is the circuit-level statement of the involution.

source_blind_decode.reconstructed_statement: For any natural number q of wires and every well-formed finite reversible program p made of X, controlled-X on distinct wires, and doubly-controlled-X on pairwise distinct wires, write E(p) for its chronological basis permutation and P(E(p))[r,c]=1 when r=E(p)(c), and 0 otherwise. Its compiled primitive program has a bare circuit C_p and a stored exact real angle theta_p. The full evaluation is D_p=exp(i theta_p) C_p, with chronological circuit multiplication C(g::rest)=C(rest)C(g). The root asserts all five statements simultaneously: (1) universally over q,p, D_p=P(E(p)) as exact complex matrices; (2) the specific compiled seven-wire primitiveAccess3Program has the stored, unreduced angle theta_star=45*pi/8, where 45/8 is real division; (3) universally over q,p, C_p=exp(i theta_p)^(-1) P(E(p)); (4) exp(i theta_star) is not 1; and (5) the bare circuit of that specific seven-wire program is not equal as a matrix to P(e_star), where e_star is the separately named primitiveAccess3BasisEquiv. The named e_star is not unfolded in this packet. The specific source program applies X0,X1, then CCX(3,0;6),CCX(6,1;2),CCX(3,0;6),CCX(3,0;1),CX(3;0),CCX(4,1;2),CX(4;1),CX(5;2), in that order. It has five CCX gates. Each supplied CCX macro accumulates two H angle fields (total pi) and four T minus three Tdagger angle fields (net pi/8), hence stores 9*pi/8; X and CX store zero. The five copies therefore store 45*pi/8. As a complex scalar, exp(i theta_star)=exp(-3*pi*i/8), while its inverse is exp(3*pi*i/8). Thus the generic bare-circuit formula applied to the displayed source program gives a nontrivial scalar multiple of that program's ideal basis permutation. The last conjunct is an exact matrix inequality, and does not say that the phase-correct full compiler output is incorrect.

source_semantics.question: Keep seven wires, a reversible program inducing a computational-basis bijection E, and the inherited definition C as the chronological ordered product of emitted primitive-gate matrices (later gates multiply on the LEFT). The historical request is exact C=P(E), hence a0/1 matrix. Assess and refute that request for the actual source compiler if it omits the program's stored phase; do not redefine the inherited bare C or silently quotient by physical global phase. A PrimitiveProgram consists of its primitive list and an exact globalPhase phi, with full denotation D=exp(i phi) C. Prove the correct compiler refinement for D using gate cases and list composition, and state the precise resulting formula for C. For the concrete primitiveAccess3ReversibleProgram (two initial X gates followed by modularAdd3ReversibleProgram, wire order address[0..2],row[0..2],work), derive the exact stored phase ledger from H,T,Tdagger and the five CCX macros, and decide whether its bare C is a0/1 permutation. Explain refinement versus definition and which full-space/basis-action, physical-global-phase and cost/cleanup conclusions follow or remain separate.
source_semantics.reference_answer:
Let P(E)[r,c]=1 if r=E(c), else0. C remains the bare list denotation as the inherited assumption requires: evalCircuit([])=I and evalCircuit(g::rest)=evalCircuit(rest) evalGate(g). A PrimitiveProgram additionally stores exact phi; evalProgram(program)=exp(i phi) C. The correct refinement is D=evalProgram(compile(program))=P(E), hence C=exp(-i phi)P(E). Exact C=P(E) holds only when exp(i phi)=1 (on the nonempty seven-wire basis), not automatically for every compiled program.

The compiler uses X,CX,CCX gate cases. X and CX compile with phase0 and their literal basis-permutation matrices. For CCX, the full H/T/Tdagger/CX macro is proved exactly: its monomial middle network restores every basis bit and gives phase-1 precisely on the111 triple (CCZ), and conjugating on the target by H gives controlled-controlled X. The source proves the bit cases, phase product, block-diagonal HZH=X and H²=I, not merely a name-based claim. Each gate case therefore satisfies evalProgram(compileGate(g))=P(E_g).

For chronology first then second, evalProgram(first.seq(second))=evalProgram(second)evalProgram(first), since lists append in chronology and stored phases add. Also P(E_second)P(E_first)=P(E_second∘E_first). Empty list givesI; induction on head/rest using these two composition identities proves the full compiler theorem. This is a refinement between independently defined primitive matrix and reversible-bijection semantics, not the definition of either one. In particular it applies to the full2^7 space, without needing a work-clean premise for the matrix equality. The separate advertised modular-address action/cleanup theorem DOES require initial work=0; refinement alone must not erase that hypothesis.

For the actual phase ledger, primitiveHProgram is chronological RZ(pi) then RY(pi/2), with stored phase pi/2, so its full denotation is H. T uses RZ(pi/4) with stored phase pi/8; Tdagger uses RZ(-pi/4) with stored phase-pi/8. A CCX macro contains two H blocks, four T blocks and three Tdagger blocks, plus phase-zero CX blocks. Thus phi_CCX=2(pi/2)+4(pi/8)-3(pi/8)=9pi/8. modularAdd3ReversibleProgram lists CCX(3,0;6),CCX(6,1;2),CCX(3,0;6),CCX(3,0;1),CX(3;0),CCX(4,1;2),CX(4;1),CX(5;2): exactly five CCX. primitiveAccess3 prepends X0,X1, both phase0. Therefore the stored exact angle evaluates to phi=45pi/8, not0; phases are accumulated exactly, not automatically reduced modulo2pi.

The complete phase-aware source theorem yields exp(i45pi/8) C=P(E), so C=exp(-i45pi/8)P(E)=exp(i3pi/8)P(E). The nonzero bare entries all equal exp(i3pi/8), which is nonreal and not1; its zeros and one-supported-position-per-row/column pattern match P(E), and it is unitary, but it is NOT an exact0/1 or real permutation matrix. The old requested equality is concretely false. The full program D IS the exact0/1 permutation and maps each basis ket to |E(c)>; bare C maps it to exp(i3pi/8)|E(c)>.

A common global phase leaves outcome probabilities and isolated pure-state rays unchanged, so the bare circuit is physically equivalent in that limited projective sense. This question instead asks exact matrix equality, where the scalar matters, especially before forming controlled operations or phase-sensitive compositions. Recording the ledger does not by itself claim a physical global-phase gate, free controlled implementation, finite-bit synthesis or a new resource bound. The seven-wire type is the concrete witness space, not an arbitrary-width gate theorem. Static proof reading is not a fresh kernel or circuit execution; separate program resource/clean-action receipts are not transferred to a different phase-omitting object.
